analysis.file_name: GS - McFerran - FLAG Series Datacentres - 6 Nov 2026.pdf
analysis.title: FLAG Series: Datacentres
key_insights: GS sees strong visibility on US data centre construction growth through 2028, with 86GW already under construction and a ~$900bn high-confidence pipeline.
GIR raises US data centre construction spend forecasts to $80bn for 2026 (from $67bn) and $100bn for 2027 (from $87bn), and introduces $125bn for 2028.
Spending could peak in 2028 but stay above 2026 levels through 2030. Post-midterm restrictions and project slippage shift activity to the right rather than reduce the total addressable market (TAM).
At roughly $3.5bn construction cost per GW, the 86GW under construction is about $300bn of spend, or ~6x 2025 US data centre construction spending.
Adding 171GW of high-probability projects takes the higher-confidence pipeline to about $900bn. Including the 293GW medium/low-probability pipeline brings the theoretical opportunity to ~$1.9tn.

Michael Ng (IT Hardware): under-construction capacity alone implies 22GW/24GW-IT of net adds in 2027/28, broadly matching his forecasts of 20GW/24GW-IT. Another 137GW-gross of high-likelihood announced capacity provides upside beyond that.
Ng sees the key risk as timing rather than cancellations, particularly in Texas, which is 20%/27% of 2027/28 under-construction additions and where a moratorium has been proposed.
Ng says delays could raise costs and push capacity to the right. IREN is most exposed, while CLS and ANET face knock-on risk from slower AI infrastructure deployment.
Adam Bubes (E&Cs): the 86GW under construction supports double-digit data centre construction spending growth in 2027 and roughly half of 2028 spending. Visibility drops materially beyond 2028.
About 55GW is scheduled to energise in 2028, so slippage without cancellation could smooth annual spending and push the cycle into 2029/30.

Democratic governors in Texas, Georgia and Michigan could introduce temporary restrictions, affecting states with roughly 45% of planned US capacity (~25% in Texas). Bubes expects moratoria to mainly hit projects that have not yet started.

Construction spending growth accelerated from +55% YoY in June to +90% in September, and 3Q starts were up strongly. Key indicators from here are project starts, new announcements and conversion of the 464GW announced pipeline into high-probability projects.

tension_points.bull_case: 86GW under construction and a ~$900bn high-confidence pipeline give visibility through 2028. GIR raises spend forecasts, and restrictions are expected to delay the cycle rather than shrink the TAM.
tension_points.bear_case: Democratic governors in Texas, Georgia and Michigan could impose temporary restrictions on states with ~45% of planned US capacity. Slippage could raise costs, and visibility drops materially beyond 2028.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Weak project starts, few new announcements, or poor conversion of the 464GW announced pipeline into high-probability projects.

theme_stances.key_argument: Post-midterm restrictions are more likely to delay and extend the cycle into 2029/30 than reduce the overall TAM.
theme_stances.evidence: midterms are more a timing risk than a TAM risk
